Sure. We covered the core vocabulary — nodes are bounded tasks, edges are real data dependencies. If no data crosses the edge, it's fake and you're wasting time running things in order. We talked about the fake-edge test: walk your workflow and ask "does this step actually need the result of the one before it?" Most workflows have two or three fake edges where steps only run sequentially because that's how they were written, not because they have to. And we covered the diamond pattern: fan out to parallel workers, reduce with code, synthesize with one final agent. That's the shape most production graphs use — breadth, not deeper reasoning. Breadth, not deeper reasoning — meaning the graph's value comes from covering more ground in parallel, not from making any single agent smarter. Like in the diamond: five researchers each tackle a different angle at the same time, rather than one researcher thinking harder about one angle. You get width — more perspectives, more sources, more coverage — but each individual node isn't doing anything a single agent couldn't do. The speedup comes from doing them all at once instead of one after another. Make sense, or want an example?

Alright, verification. The part most people skip — and what separates a real graph from an expensive toy. Models miss most of their own mistakes. A model grading its own work is too easy on itself. The rule: never let the agent that did the work check the work. You place a separate verifier node on the edge, and its only job is to try to kill the finding before it moves on. Critical part: the verifier needs a clean context. If you give it the same conversation the worker had, it's not checking anything — it's just nodding along to itself in a different font. Does that land, or feel abstract?
So in short, it this about having agents not check their own work?

Exactly. That's the core principle. But there's a second piece that's easy to miss: the verifier can't just be a different agent — it needs a different *context*. If both agents see the same chat history, the verifier is primed to agree. It has to come in fresh, seeing only the output and the rules, nothing else. That's what makes it actually independent. Your harness is a one-node diamond. The planner is the fan-out decision — it decides what to build. The generator is the single worker node doing the actual work. The evaluator is the verification edge — blind to the generator's context, trying to kill the output before it passes. And if it passes, that's your synthesize step — the work ships. In a full graph, you'd just multiply the generator node — ten parallel generators instead of one, each building a different piece, then one evaluator checking all of them, then one synthesizer pulling it together. Same skeleton, wider. Make sense?
Why wouldn't you why wouldn't you want multiple
evaluators?

You *do* want multiple evaluators — that's exactly what the document recommends. Three different lenses catch what ten identical ones miss. The pattern is called "perspective-diverse verify" — give each evaluator a distinct job. One checks correctness, one checks security, one checks reproducibility. Or in your case with code: one checks if it runs, one checks if it's maintainable, one checks if it matches the spec. Diversity of perspective is the point. A single evaluator is the minimum — multiple evaluators with different lenses is the robust version. Does that change how you'd want to set up your harness?
Do you need an evaluator that checks everything at a high level?

Not necessarily. If three evaluators each check their lens and all three pass, the work is good — you don't need a fourth agent to re-check what the other three already confirmed. The exception is if their findings *conflict* — like one says "this is correct" and another says "this violates the spec." Then you might need a tiebreaker or a synthesizer to resolve it. But if they're checking genuinely separate things — correctness, security, maintainability — and each one passes independently, you're done. The high-level check is implicit: all three said yes. Ah — yeah, that's a real failure mode. It's called "false independence" in the document. The nodes look independent because their prompts never mention each other, but they're actually touching the same file, or they create pieces that don't fit together. The fix is twofold. One: give each worker its own isolated workspace so they can't overwrite each other — that's the worktree pattern Bun's team used. Two: add a final integration check that's *not* about any individual piece, but about whether the pieces compose. That could be "does the whole thing build?" or "do the interfaces match?"or "does the integration test pass?"That's your holistic evaluator — it checks the seams, not the parts. Does that address it?

You're hitting the limit of what verification can do. An agent can check "does this code run?" or "does this match the spec?"— those are answerable. But "is this the right architecture?"or "will this scale?" or "is this the smart choice?"— that's judgment, and the document is pretty clear: graphs buy breadth, not better judgment. You can build a judge panel — generate three different approaches, score them, pick the winner — but that's still just picking the best of what the model came up with, not guaranteeing it's actually good. The honest answer: if the decision matters, that's where you belong. The graph can generate options and check constraints, but the final "is this right?"is still you. Right — and that's actually the human gate principle the document covers later. You don't approve every step, because that kills the graph's value. But you *do* approve where a mistake would be expensive to undo. The irreversible stuff — anything that ships, touches a customer, or sets the architecture for the next six months. The graph runs wide and fast, but the gate sits where judgment matters. That's the balance. Ready to keep going, or want to sit with this piece?

Alright — so after verification, the document covers failure modes. Three big ones. First: context collapse. You fan out to a thousand nodes, then try to feed all their outputs into one final step, and you blow past the context window before synthesis even starts. The fix is layered fan-in — batch results, summarize each batch, then combine summaries. Never dump the raw pile into one prompt. Second failure mode: false independence, which we just talked about. And third: silent node failure. In a chain, one failure stops everything — annoying but obvious. In a graph, one dead node among two hundred can slip into a report that looks complete. Let's go one at a time.

First one: context collapse. You fan out to a bunch of parallel workers — say, fifty researchers each gathering data. Then you try to feed all fifty outputs into one final agent to write the summary. But all fifty results together are too big for the context window, so the whole thing crashes before synthesis even starts. The fix: don't merge everything at once. Batch it — summarize ten results at a time, then combine those five summaries into one. You layer the fan-in instead of doing it all in one step. Make sense?
What is our goal here?

Good question — stepping back. The goal of this section is to know how graphs fail in practice, so you don't build something that looks right but breaks at scale. These aren't theoretical — they're the patterns that actually bit teams in production. Context collapse, false independence, silent failures. If you know the failure modes upfront, you design around them instead of discovering them after you've already built the thing. Does that frame help, or are you asking what *your* goal is for this session?
No. I wanna know what the goal of like, or guess I still don't understand
what you were saying. About batching them. Batching what? What are we batching?

The outputs from the parallel workers. Say you have fifty researchers, and each one writes a report. You can't feed all fifty reports into one agent at once — that's too much text, the context window can't hold it. So instead: take the first ten reports, have one agent summarize those ten into one summary. Take the next ten, summarize those. Do that five times. Now you have five summaries instead of fifty full reports. *Those* five fit in the context window, so you can feed them to a final agent that writes the overall synthesis. You're batching the fifty outputs into groups of ten, shrinking them, then combining the shrunken versions. Does that click?
When you do this, don't do you lose some context by batching then?

Yeah — you lose detail. That's the tradeoff. The question is whether you need that detail in the final output. If the goal is a high-level synthesis — "what are the five main themes across all this research? "— then batching works fine. You're deliberately compressing. But if the final output needs specific facts from all fifty sources, then batching doesn't work. You'd need a different approach — maybe structured extraction where each worker outputs just the key facts in a schema, so fifty structured outputs are small enough to merge without summarizing. The fix depends on what you're trying to preserve. Does that distinction help?
Yeah.

Three main ones in this section: context collapse, false independence, and silent node failure. We just covered context collapse. Want to keep going through the other two, or shift to something else?
Can you describe why it's called
context collapse?

Because the context window collapses under the weight of too much input. You're trying to stuff more text into the final prompt than the model can actually hold — the window has a limit, you exceed it, and the whole thing fails. It "collapses" in the sense that the synthesis step can't happen at all. The term is just describing what breaks: the context. Make sense?
When I hear that you know, an LLM model has increased its context window, does that mean it can
handle more context?
Or that just you can feed it more?

Both — they're the same thing. A bigger context window means the model can hold more text in memory at once. So you can feed it more *and* it can handle more. The catch is that even with a huge window, models still get worse at using information buried in the middle — that's called "lost in the middle." So a 200k token window doesn't mean you should actually use all 200k. But yeah, bigger window = more input capacity. Does that answer it, or are you asking something else?
It's still not super clear to me.
So its cape its ability the model's ability
to remember and use more context also improves as the context window
increases.

Not automatically, no. The window size is just capacity — how much text fits. But the model's ability to actually *use* all that text effectively doesn't scale perfectly with window size. Even with a million-token window, models still struggle to pull out a detail from token 500,000 when answering at token 999,999. The "lost in the middle" problem persists.
What is the work
done to
improve that?

A few things. One is training specifically on long-context tasks, so the model learns to attend to distant tokens. Another is architectural changes — like sparse attention or hierarchical memory — so the model doesn't have to process every token equally. And retrieval augmentation helps too: instead of dumping everything into context, you search and pull just the relevant pieces. But honestly, the most reliable fix is still what we talked about earlier: don't rely on the model holding everything at once. Structure the input, batch it, or use code to filter before the model ever sees it. The engineering pattern is more robust than waiting for the model to get better. Does that land?
Say that one more time. Very concisely.
The window is capacity, not capability. Models still struggle to use everything they can hold. The fix is engineering — batch, filter, structure — not waiting for better models.
Okay. Let's move on.

Second failure mode: false independence. Two nodes look independent because their prompts don't mention each other, but they both write to the same file or hit the same rate-limited API. That's a hidden edge — they actually depend on each other, you just didn't see it. When Bun's team first tried this, agents shared one workspace and overwrote each other's changes. The fix: give every worker its own isolated space. In practice, that means separate git worktrees — each agent works in its own copy, does its thing, then merges cleanly. Make sense?

So does that mean Eve So the the solution to give each worker its own own work was that so the the workers might still be working on the same files, but they're able to merge cleanly. Is that correct?

Exactly. Each worker gets its own copy of the repo in a separate worktree. They can both edit the same file without stepping on each other, because they're editing *different copies*. Then after they're done, you merge the changes — and if there's a conflict, you handle it explicitly, instead of one agent silently overwriting the other. The isolation prevents the collision. The merge is where you reconcile. Does that click?
Yeah.

Cool. Third failure mode: silent node failure. In a linear chain, if one step breaks, everything stops — annoying, but obvious. In a graph with two hundred parallel nodes, one dead node can slip through. The final report looks complete, but it's actually missing data from the node that quietly failed. The fix: every merge step counts its inputs. If you fanned out to fifty workers, the merge should check "did I get fifty results?"If it only got forty-nine, flag the gap instead of quietly running on incomplete data. Make sense?

You'd think so, but in practice it's easy to miss. If you're using something like `Promise.allSettled()` instead of `Promise.all()`, failed nodes resolve to null instead of throwing. The code keeps running. Or if you're batching results from a queue and one worker times out, the batch just moves on. The merge step sees *some* results and proceeds. Unless you explicitly count and compare, the gap is silent. The system doesn't crash — it just quietly delivers partial work. That's why the document calls it out: it *should* be obvious, but the default behavior in most async patterns lets failures slip through. Does that make it clearer?

It applies to both, but it's more dangerous in research-type tasks. In software, you usually have a build step or test suite that catches missing pieces — if a module didn't generate, the build fails. But in research, summarization, or content generation, there's no automatic check. A report based on forty-nine sources instead of fifty still *reads* fine. It's complete-looking but incomplete. So the silent failure is harder to catch. That's where the explicit count matters. In code, you often get the failure for free. In open-ended work, you have to build it in. Make sense?
